title: Films for high school film elective

commenti.body:
Zama (2017) depicts the colonialism & steady unraveling of an officer of the Spanish crown in 18th-century South America.

https://www.nytimes.com/2018/04/12/movies/review-zama-lucrecia-martel.html

"Hero" (2002) - all those primary colors in the service of storytelling  
  
"The Social Network" (2010) - a Royal Regatta race as spectacle 

"Shin Godzilla" (2016) - repurposing 3/11 disaster imagery to critique bureaucratic inaction

My high school film class (which was great) was built around a few eras, a few genres, and a few specific directors, but to add to it, if you were to also pick some crowd-pleasing modern hits, and then demonstrate their influences by showing some older movies that influenced them technique/structure/theme-wise, that could really get their gears turning.

The Dark Knight (they've all probably seen it) is influenced by Michael Mann's Heat (95) in ways that allow you to discuss color theory, pacing, act structure, set pieces, conflict, & cinematography (each movie's 'face off' between detective and criminal is shot similarly). Kubrick's The Killing influences it as well, and that's a very tight paced 50s movie they won't expect to like.

Interstellar is another Nolan movie they will know/care about, that shares so much DNA with 2001: A Space Odyssey, so you could get multiple class periods out of symbolism and story structure there, even if you didn't make them sit through it.

Dune 2 and Lawrence of Arabia are different genres, on different planets, with highly similar story structures and themes.

Fantastic Mr Fox would go over well, and is a good character piece with plenty of shot composition choices to talk about.

How old are these students? What your supervisor may be open to would vary greatly depending on if they are freshmen or seniors. 

Without knowing that, I would be reluctant to point you towards any specific films, instead maybe some specific concepts to cover. Like the Kuleshov Effect. There’s a [great interview with Hitchcock](https://youtu.be/96xx383lpiI) that explains the principle.  Sammy filming and editing Ditch Day in *The Fablemans (2022)* (specifically the sea gulls and ice cream) is a great example of how editing constructs meaning. 

You could crib some ideas from [this NerdWriter1 video](https://youtu.be/3hZ_ZyzCO24) about *Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (2004)*. 

And there’s always the excellent [Every Frame a Painting](http://www.youtube.com/@everyframeapainting) series for additional ideas.

I don't have rosters at this time, but the class is theoretically open to grades 9-12 - though typically upperclassmen are the ones that have flexibility in their schedule for electives.

Thanks for the links I will check these out!

My question would be how do you define "modern" and "classic"?  I have my ideas as to what they mean, but they're probably a lot different than yours.  Also, how many films are you showing?  That's just as important.

Back when I took a film class in high school we were allowed to watch R-rated movies because in order to take the class your parent signed a waiver saying they were okay with it.  I'd see if that's an option because that'd really open you up.  Also, I'd see what they mean by "modern".

That class was the first time I saw Raging Bull and that movie really opened my eyes about film in general.  We also watched Strangers on a Train and Hope and Glory.  There are plenty of movies I'd want to show in a film class, but I'd say if you can swing it, anything by Scorsese would work really well as far as being accessible to younger people goes.

I’m in Highschool and really into Film some of my personal favorites are Parasite,Taxi Driver,One Flew Over The Cuckoos Nest,Whiplash,saving private ryan,Good Will Hunting,The ShawShank Redemption and Silence of the Lambs

You should probably chat me on this. It would take me a while to come up with appropriate recommendations so I would want as much information as possible before I devote all this time to this project.

For since quicker discussions, I’ve used Ah-Ha’s video “Take On Me” to demonstrate 3 Act Structure used in storytelling, and Avril Lavigne’s video “Girlfriend “ to discuss anti-heroes, villains, and dovetail into the idea of the unreliable narrator.

Patrick H. Willems has a nice 90 minute video about how to analyze a film using. Highly recommended 
https://youtu.be/ahHIifcFyqk?feature=shared

As for movies-it depends on if you are allowed R-rated films or not. I’m guessing “not really, but maybe?” 

Something movies that are enjoyable for high-schoolers, has interesting cinematography and thematic elements:

Raiders of the Lost Ark (students: what? There’s no CGI???)
Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (dealing trauma) 
The Tree of Life (…actually…maybe not? I mean, *I* think it’s great, with nice cinematography and themes, but high-schoolers? May be not).
Les Miserables (cinematography, themes of the redeeming power of forgiveness)
Dunkirk (non-linear storytelling)
Barbie 
Black Panther: Wakanda Forever (not a great movie, but good for themes like healing from loss)
Get Out
La La Land (character development and the little subtle things that *don’t * develop)
…if somehow you can get approval to show it - Amélie, buuuut for high school you might want to steer clear of this, even though I think it hella fun and something hs kids could probably relate to 

Just a few
